(CNN) -- After a nearly decade-long effort, the National Congress of Black Women on Tuesday honored Sojourner Truth by making her the first African-American woman to have a memorial bust in the U.S. Capitol. Speaker Nancy Pelosi and first lady Michelle Obama applaud the unveiling of the Sojourner Truth bust. Truth, whose given name was Isabella Baumfree, was a slave who became one of the most respected abolitionists and women's rights activists. "One could only imagine what Sojourner Truth, an outspoken, tell-it-like-it-is kind of woman ... what she would have to say about this incredible gathering," first lady Michelle Obama said at the Celebration of Truth ceremony. "We are all here because, as my husband says time and time again, we stand on the shoulders of giants like Sojourner Truth." "And just as Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott would be pleased to know that we have a woman serving as the speaker of the House of Representatives, I hope that Sojourner Truth would be proud to see me, a descendant of slaves, serving as the first lady of the United States of America," she said. Dignitaries and congressional leaders, including Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, House Republican Leader John Boehner and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, attended the ceremony marking the unveiling of the statue. Along with musical performances, actress Cicely Tyson recited "Ain't I A Woman," Truth's famous 1851 speech to a women's rights convention. Clinton and Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee, who worked together to draft legislation to commission the bust, were among speakers who paid tribute to the late C. Delores Tucker, former chairwoman of the NCBW, who spearheaded the effort for the Truth memorial. "What a wonderful day it is to be here in Emancipation Hall for this great occasion when Sojourner Truth takes her rightful place alongside the heroes who have helped to shape our nation's history," Clinton said. "Today, she takes her place in this Capitol, and we are the better for it," Clinton said. "She is a sojourner of truth, by truth, and for truth. And her words, her example and her legacy will never perish from this earth, so long as men and women stand up and say loudly and clearly, 'We hear you echoing down through the years of history. We believe that your journey is not yet over, and we will make the rest of that journey with you.' " The bronze statue, which was crafted by Los Angeles, California, sculptor Artis Lane, will stand in Emancipation Hall at the Capitol Visitor Center. "All the visitors in the U.S. Capitol will hear the story of brave women who endured the greatest of humanity's indignities. They'll hear the story of Sojourner Truth, who didn't allow those indignities to destroy her spirit, who fought for her own freedom and then used her powers ... to help others," Michelle Obama said. "The power of this bust will not just be in the metal that delineates Sojourner Truth's face; it will also be in the message that defines her legacy. Forevermore, in the halls of one of our country's greatest monuments of liberty and equality, justice and freedom, Sojourner Truth's story will be told again and again and again and again." In 1997, Congress passed a special act that called for relocating the Portrait Monument from the Capitol basement to the rotunda. The 7.5-ton statue depicts three leaders of the suffragette movement -- Anthony, Stanton and Mott. A group called the Sojourner Truth Crusade was upset about the statue's relocation because it didn't incorporate Truth. After Congress agreed to go ahead with a move, advocates proposed commissioning a new statue that would include Truth. In 2006, Congress passed a bill to honor the abolitionist with her own memorial.

Speakers emphasized that Truth’s activism bridged causes that are sometimes treated separately: racial justice, women’s equality, labor rights, religious freedom and human dignity.

Born into slavery in Ulster County, New York, Truth endured forced labor and family separation before escaping with her infant daughter in 1826. She later became the first Black woman known to successfully sue a white man in a U.S. court when she fought for the return of her son Peter, who had been illegally sold. In the decades that followed, she traveled widely, speaking against slavery and advocating for women’s rights at a time when Black women were often excluded even from reform movements.

Her most famous public appearance came at the 1851 Women’s Rights Convention in Akron, Ohio, where she delivered remarks later remembered as “Ain’t I a Woman?” Though the exact wording of the speech has been debated by historians, its moral force remains central to her legacy: Truth challenged both racism and sexism, insisting that Black women’s experiences be recognized in the fight for equality.

The placement of her bust in the Capitol also prompted reflection on who is honored in public monuments and whose stories have been marginalized. For generations, the Capitol’s statuary and portraiture largely celebrated presidents, military figures and political leaders—most of them white men. The recognition of Sojourner Truth signals a broader shift toward commemorating reformers, activists and women whose contributions helped expand democracy itself.

Civil rights leaders in attendance praised the unveiling as a moment of historical correction. Several speakers noted that Truth did not hold elected office, command an army or sign legislation, yet her words and witness helped change the nation’s moral trajectory.

“She represents the power of the citizen’s voice,” one speaker said. “She reminds us that history is not made only by those with titles, but by those with courage.”

The ceremony also carried particular significance for women serving in government. Lawmakers present described Truth’s legacy as foundational to the opportunities women now have in public life, while acknowledging that barriers remain. Her bust, they said, will stand as a reminder to future generations of leaders that the rights enjoyed today were secured through struggle.

As the covering was drawn away and Lane’s bronze sculpture was revealed, the crowd responded with applause, some rising to their feet. The bust’s unveiling was both solemn and celebratory—a recognition of suffering endured, battles fought and progress made.

For Michelle Obama, Pelosi, Clinton and the many dignitaries gathered, the day was not only about commemorating Sojourner Truth’s place in history. It was also about affirming the continued relevance of her message.

More than a century after her death in 1883, Truth’s voice continues to echo in debates over race, gender, citizenship and equality. With Artis Lane’s bust now standing in the Capitol, that voice gains a permanent place in the nation’s symbolic heart.

“Sojourner Truth asked America to live up to its promises,” Obama said. “Today, we honor her by remembering that the work she began is still ours to carry forward.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a journalistic summary of the decade-long effort to place a Sojourner Truth memorial in the Capitol, including the role of C. Delores Tucker, Congress, and the suffrage monument controversy.
counterfactuals.output:
For more than a decade, the campaign to place Sojourner Truth in the U.S. Capitol unfolded as both a memorial project and a dispute over who had been left out of the nation’s official story of women’s rights.

The effort was driven in large part by C. Delores Tucker, the Pennsylvania civil-rights activist and founder of the National Congress of Black Women. In the 1990s, Tucker and allied women’s groups pressed Congress to honor Truth, the formerly enslaved abolitionist, preacher and women’s-rights advocate best known for her 1851 “Ain’t I a Woman?” speech. Their campaign argued that the Capitol’s commemorative landscape celebrated the suffrage movement while largely excluding Black women who had fought slavery and sexism at the same time.

The push became entangled with a separate controversy over the Capitol’s historic suffrage monument, officially the Portrait Monument to Lucretia Mott, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony. The marble sculpture, donated in 1921, had long been relegated to the Capitol Crypt before women’s groups campaigned to move it to the Rotunda. Some advocates proposed adding Sojourner Truth to the monument, partly to correct the racial narrowness of the original tribute. But that idea sparked objections from historians, preservationists and members of Congress who argued that altering the artwork would distort the original sculpture and its history. Others saw the resistance as another example of Black women being asked to wait for recognition.

Congress ultimately moved the suffrage monument to the Rotunda in 1997 but barred changes to it. That decision effectively separated the two issues: the original suffrage monument would remain intact, and advocates would seek a distinct memorial for Truth.

Tucker continued lobbying for that separate tribute, but she died in 2005 before seeing the effort completed. Congress later authorized the placement of a bust of Sojourner Truth in the Capitol, with the project funded privately and supported by the National Congress of Black Women and other advocates. Sculptor Artis Lane created the bronze bust.

On April 28, 2009, the memorial was unveiled in Emancipation Hall in the Capitol Visitor Center. The ceremony, attended by congressional leaders and First Lady Michelle Obama, marked the first time an African American woman was honored with a bust in the U.S. Capitol. The installation was widely described not only as a tribute to Truth, but also as a belated correction to a commemorative record that had long separated the histories of abolition, women’s suffrage and Black women’s leadership.
